meta.title: Hemp, THC and alcohol rules, 18 days of posts
meta.subject: the regulation of hemp-derived THC products and beverage alcohol in Texas — the THC ban and its alternatives, Lt. Gov. Patrick's push and the industry's response, TABC rules, beer and spirits distribution, alcohol-to-go and alcohol taxes
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 18, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas THC, hemp and alcohol regulation, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Ban feeds cartels, black market
lanes.description: Prohibiting hemp THC won't end demand; it pushes Texans from licensed local shops to cartels and unregulated dealers, so Texas should regulate rather than prohibit.

lanes.label: Ban kills small businesses, jobs
lanes.description: The THC ban and new licensing fees destroy Texas hemp shops, farmers and manufacturers, costing jobs and tax revenue and leaving billions on the table.

lanes.label: Veterans, patients, and personal freedom
lanes.description: Adults, veterans and patients rely on hemp products for relief and have a right to choose, so the ban is government overreach into personal liberty.

lanes.label: Patrick's ban as electoral liability
lanes.description: Dan Patrick and Republicans drove the ban (SB3, Abbott's order), and Democrats and hemp advocates use it to mobilize voters against them in the 2026 elections.

lanes.label: Lawsuits, TABC rules, and enforcement
lanes.description: The fight over THC rules is playing out in the courts and enforcement, including smokable/THCA bans, TABC and DSHS rules, appeals, lab/COA disputes, smoke shop raids and the federal deadline.

lanes.label: Protecting kids and public safety
lanes.description: Restricting hemp THC is needed to protect children and communities from unregulated, potent or contaminated products, illicit shops and drug-linked crime.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Team Talarico
posts.text:
.@JamesTalarico on Texas officially banning THC:

“This bill is insane.

Texans aren’t going to stop smoking weed and eating edibles because politicians in Austin say so. Texans will still use THC — but instead of getting it safely from a local small business, they’ll go back to getting it from the black market. From the drug cartels.

This ban is a gift to the cartels.

We are now telling full-grown adults how to live their lives. This is the nanny state at its worst; this is big government at its worst. 

Instead of fully funding our schools, guaranteeing healthcare, or making childcare more affordable — this Legislature is focused on banning a product that gives people a little peace. 

We’re making people’s lives harder, not easier.

I want to leave you with a quote: ‘It is time to end needless arrests and incarcerations of adults for small amounts of marijuana for personal use.’ That wasn’t a Democrat. That was President Donald Trump.

To my Republican colleagues, I’m asking you to oppose the cartels, stand with President Trump, and vote no on this insane bill.”

posts.name: TexasBlue
posts.text:
Outspent and unknown, Democrat Vikki Goodwin gives Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick his toughest race yet https://t.co/Iwu3O5F5cv By 6 p.m. on a recent Monday, Vikki Goodwin had sat through a five-hour Texas House insurance committee hearing, worked the phones to thank campaign donors for their latest checks, sat for an interview with a cannabis podcast where she bashed Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick’s push to ban THC products, and was en route to a mixer for a fellow Democrat running for Congress.

Such is half a day in the life of Texas’ Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor, who is taking on one of the state’s top GOP kingmakers on a shoestring campaign budget. But despite his comparatively massive war chest and the name recognition from nearly 12 years in statewide office, Patrick is running like he feels the heat more than ever before. Confronting a scrappy opponent and a rough midterm climate for the GOP, the state’s second-in-command has been forced to go after Goodwin by name in speeches and attack ads — a distinction rarely, if ever, afforded to his past Democratic foes — while warning Republican voters and peers the threat is real.
